title: The federal government has announced major changes to investment rules for super funds that will allow them to invest more broadly.read more
full_text:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has announced three major reforms to investment rules surrounding the performance test for superannuation funds.
In his keynote address at the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia (ASFA) Conference in Melbourne today, Chalmers said the changes were intended to strengthen the test and not water it down.
The three main reforms are a new benchmark for emerging asset classes, bringing more products under the test and improvements in how it is administered.
Under the changes, superannuation fund trustees can choose to use the new benchmark for up to 5 per cent of their portfolio, something Chalmers suggested has the potential to unlock up to $90 billion of investments in emerging assets. The new benchmark will be set at a margin above the consumer price index with different levels for growth and defensive assets.
“The new benchmark is voluntary and the central obligation of trustees to act in members’ best interests is unchanged. It uses a sector‑neutral definition for eligible assets, focused on where existing benchmarking options fall short. And it will be based on independent advice from the Australian Government Actuary and administered by APRA (Australian Prudential Regulation Authority),” Chalmers told delegates at the conference.
The changes were broadly welcomed by industry associations, including the Financial Services Council (FSC) and ASFA.
“The Treasurer’s announcement today that the performance test will include growth and defensive CPI plus X benchmarks for a defined portion of portfolios will give superannuation funds greater scope to invest in assets that are not appropriately captured by the current benchmarks, but still require funds to act in members’ best financial interests,” FSC chief executive Blake Briggs noted.
ASFA chief executive Mary Delahunty agreed superannuation funds and their members would benefit from the changes.
“These reforms will support super funds in delivering the best-possible long-term returns for Australians, while strengthening the performance test as a consumer-comparison tool,” Delahunty pointed out.
The government is also extending the performance test to externally directed products, or products a third party manages instead of a trustee, where they are comparable with those already in the test. Chalmers estimated this would provide protections for up to 1.4 million more members.
“Having more platform products in scope will stabilise the fee benchmarks and provide a more reliable basis for comparison,” he explained.
